newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Amnesty slams sentencing of Brazil landless leader.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty slams sentencing of Brazil landless leader.

text.p: Rights group Amnesty International said on Thursday it was "outraged" by the sentence of 26 years in prison given to a leader of Brazil's radical Landless Movement (MST) who was convicted of murder.
"This charge was clearly politically motivated and obviously intended to harass members of the landless rural workers' movement," Amnesty said in a statement.

A jury in Espirito Santo state on Wednesday found Jose Rainha guilty of the 1989 murders of a local farmer and a police officer who died in an ambush. At the time, Rainha was a leader of landless rural workers in the region.

Amnesty said five witnesses testified that Rainha was hundreds of miles away in the northeastern state of Ceara at the time of the ambush, but prosecution lawyers urged the jury to convict him on his membership in the MST alone, it said.

The seven-member jury found Rainha guilty of organising a group of landless workers to kill the two men and of aiding the escape of members of the alleged gang. A judge sentenced the MST leader to 26 years in jail but allowed him to stay free pending a retrial in September. Retrials in Brazil are automatic in the case of sentences of more than 20 years.
"If Jose Rainha is imprisoned, we will consider him a prisoner of conscience and demand his immediate and unconditional release," Amnesty said.

Rainha is one of the most senior members of the MST's leadership. He was included in a delegation that met President Fernando Henrique Cardoso in April after a massive demonstration in Brasilia to demand faster land reform.

Once an illiterate labourer, he rose through the MST's ranks by organising and leading invasions of unused, private farmland. Hundreds of MST members gathered outside the courtroom in Pedro Canaria in support of their leader and greeted the verdict with an eerie silence.

The Pastoral Land Commission (CPT), a Catholic Church group, also saw political motives behind the trial. "Even after the defence got relatives of the victims off the jury most of the jurors were linked to big landowners of the area in their hatred for the landless," it said in a statement.

The CPT has documented the killing of 976 rural workers in clashes over land in the last 12 years and said only 58 have resulted in court cases. Brazil has one of the world's most unfair land distribution ratios with about half of all arable land in the hands of just two percent of landowners.
